For how can it be said her "warfare was accomplished," when as yet the galling yoke of Antiochus and also of Rome was before them? The "double for her sins" must refer to the twofold captivity, the Assyrian and the Roman; at the coming close of this latter dispersion, and then only, can her "iniquity" be said to be "pardoned," or fully expiated [Houbigant]. Messiah is the antitypical Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mt 2:15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>). Otherwise (cry unto her) "that she shall receive (blessings) of the Lord's hand double to the punishment of all her sins" (so "sin" is used, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.19">Zec 14:19</reference>, Margin) [Lowth]. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9051"/><div sID="gen15264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9051"/><hi type="bold">3. crieth in the wilderness--</hi>So the Septuagint and <reference osisRef="Matt.3.3">Mt 3:3</reference> connect the words. The Hebrew accents, however, connect them thus: "In the wilderness prepare ye," &c., and the parallelism also requires this, "Prepare ye in the wilderness," answering to "make straight in the desert." Matthew was entitled, as under inspiration, to vary the connection, so as to bring out another sense, included in the Holy Spirit's intention; in <reference osisRef="Matt.3.1">Mt 3:1</reference>, "John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness," answers thus to "The voice of one crying in the wilderness." Maurer takes the participle as put for the finite verb (so in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Is 40:6</reference>), "A voice crieth." The clause, "in the wilderness," alludes to Israel's passage through it from Egypt to Canaan (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.7">Psa 68:7</reference>), Jehovah being their leader; so it shall be at the coming restoration of Israel, of which the restoration from Babylon was but a type (not the full realization; for their way from it was not through the "wilderness"). Where John preached (namely, in the wilderness; the type of this earth, a moral wilderness), there were the hearers who are ordered to prepare the way of the Lord, and there was to be the coming of the Lord [Bengel]. John, though he was immediately followed by the suffering Messiah, is rather the herald of the coming reigning Messiah, as Mal 4:5, 6 ("before the great and dreadful day of the Lord"), proves. <reference osisRef="Matt.17.11">Mt 17:11</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.3.21">Ac 3:21</reference>) implies that John is not exclusively meant; and that though in one sense Elias has come, in another he is yet to come. John was the figurative Elias, coming "in the spirit and power of Elias" (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Lu 1:17</reference>); <reference osisRef="John.1.21">Joh 1:21</reference>, where John the Baptist denies that he was the actual Elias, accords with this view. Mal 4:5, 6 cannot have received its exhaustive fulfilment in John; the Jews always understood it of the literal Elijah. As there is another consummating advent of Messiah Himself, so perhaps there is to be of his forerunner Elias, who also was present at the transfiguration.<div eID="gen15264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>Hebrew, Jehovah; as this is applied to Jesus, He must be Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.3">Mt 3:3</reference>). <div eID="gen15265" type="x-p"/>

The gospel minister must "open his mouth boldly" ( Pr 29:25 ; Ep 6:19 ). Behold-- especially at His second coming ( Zec 12:10 ; 14:5 ).

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 40 Is 40:1-31 . Second Part of the Prophecies of Isaiah. The former were local and temporary in their reference. These belong to the distant future, and are world-wide in their interest; the deliverance from Babylon under Cyrus, which he here foretells by prophetic suggestion, carries him on to the greater deliverance under Messiah, the Saviour of Jews and Gentiles in the present eclectic Church, and the restorer of Israel and Head of the world-wide kingdom, literal and spiritual, ultimately. As Assyria was the hostile world power in the former part, which refers to Isaiah's own time, so Babylon is so in the latter part, which refers to a period long subsequent. The connecting link, however, is furnished ( Is 39:6 ) at the close of the former part. The latter part was written in the old age of Isaiah, as appears from the greater mellowness of style and tone which pervades it; it is less fiery and more tender and gentle than the former part.
